content: The use of erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) has been shown to benefit patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). However, the effectiveness and safety of short-acting epoetins, particularly when administered in larger doses at reduced frequencies, as well as the use of newer epoetins and biosimilars, remain uncertain. This review aimed to assess the benefits and risks associated with different administration routes, dosing frequencies, and dosages of short-acting epoetins (such as epoetin alpha and epoetin beta) for treating anaemia in adults and children with CKD who are not on dialysis. The search for relevant studies was conducted using the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Specialised Register up to September 12, 2016. This database includes studies identified through systematic searches of CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, conference proceedings, and clinical trial registries. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing various frequencies, routes, doses, and types of short-acting ESAs in CKD patients were included in the review. Two authors independently determined study eligibility, while four authors assessed the risk of bias and extracted data. Results for dichotomous outcomes were expressed as risk ratios (RR) or risk differences (RD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). For continuous outcomes, mean differences (MD) with 95% CI were used. Statistical analyses were performed using a random-effects model. A total of 14 RCTs involving 2616 participants were identified. Nine of these studies were multi-centre trials, and two included children. The overall risk of bias was high in most studies. Only three studies demonstrated adequate random sequence generation, and only two had a low risk of bias for allocation concealment. Blinding of participants and personnel was at low risk of bias in one study, while blinding of outcome assessment was judged to be at low risk in 13 studies, as outcomes were primarily based on laboratory results. Attrition bias was low in eight studies, and selective reporting bias was low in six studies. The interventions compared included the following: 1. Epoetin alpha or beta administered at different frequencies but with the same total dose (six studies). 2. Epoetin alpha administered at the same frequency but with different total doses (two studies). 3. Epoetin alpha administered intravenously versus subcutaneously (one study). 4. Epoetin alpha or beta compared with other epoetins or biosimilars (five studies). One study compared both different frequencies of epoetin alpha at the same total dose and the same frequency with different total doses. Data from only seven of the 14 studies were included in the meta-analyses. No significant differences in final haemoglobin (Hb) levels were observed when comparing: Dosing every two weeks versus weekly dosing (four studies, 785 participants: MD -0.20 g/dL, 95% CI -0.33 to -0.07). Four-weekly dosing versus two-weekly dosing (three studies, 671 participants: MD -0.16 g/dL, 95% CI -0.43 to 0.10). Different total doses administered at the same frequency (four-weekly administration: one study, 144 participants: MD 0.17 g/dL, 95% CI -0.19 to 0.53). Five studies evaluated different interventions: One study compared epoetin theta with epoetin alpha and found no significant differences in Hb levels (288 participants: MD -0.02 g/dL, 95% CI -0.25 to 0.21). One study reported significantly higher pain scores with subcutaneous epoetin alpha compared to epoetin beta. Two studies (165 participants) compared epoetin delta with epoetin alpha, but no results were available because the pharmaceutical company withdrew epoetin delta for commercial reasons. One study comparing the biosimilar HX575 with epoetin alpha was terminated after patients receiving HX575 subcutaneously developed anti-epoetin antibodies, and no results were available. Adverse events were poorly reported across all studies and did not differ significantly between comparisons. Mortality data were adequately detailed in only four studies, and only one study included data on quality of life. The authors concluded that administering epoetin alpha at higher doses over extended intervals (two or four weeks) is not inferior to more frequent dosing intervals in maintaining final Hb levels in non-dialysed CKD patients. No significant differences in adverse effects were observed. However, the methodological quality of the data is low, and differences in efficacy and safety cannot be ruled out. Further large, well-designed RCTs focusing on patient-centred outcomes are needed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of administering large doses of short-acting ESAs, including biosimilars of epoetin alpha, less frequently compared to smaller, more frequent doses in both children and adults with CKD who are not on dialysis.
